title: Rules Bench
context: Grade 4, and the chapter stops calculating here to look at what is always true. An adult sees two properties and four shortcuts. What the page is actually doing is separating a rule about places from a rule about shapes: adding a thousand raises the thousands digit, and a child who has learnt it as the digit third from the end will raise the wrong one the moment the number gets longer. The true or false question the page closes on is built to catch exactly that, and its printed wrong answer is the one most children reach for.

writeup.why: Find out what you are allowed to change about a sum without changing its answer, and which single digit moves when you add a round amount.
writeup.look: Two column mats side by side sharing one set of number cards, with a step bay and a ring of circles below them.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Rules Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many cards are standing on each mat, two numbers side by side in ink, so a bracket that turns three cards into two can be read there without counting the mat over; on the last two phases it carries the number the step bay began with and, under it, the amount being added, written in words. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The card tray runs along the top of the working area, 1086 by 88 at 64,202, holding the phase's number cards 150 by 64 at a pitch of 166; a card drawn out of the tray leaves its outline behind and the outline refills, so the same card can be dealt to both mats at once. The two mats are 510 by 256 at 64,300 and at 640,300, the same rectangle twice: a heading row 36 tall of five ruled cells reading TTh, Th, H, T and O, a carry strip 34 tall above the heading row where a carried digit stands small and vermilion over the column it is being added into, two addend rows 56 tall on the first phase and three on the second, a rule 4 tall under the last addend, and the sum row 56 tall under the rule with its digits in green. Between the mats, 66 wide at 574,300, runs the compare rail: it stays blank until both sums are written, and when the two sum rows read alike it closes as a single bar across the gap with the word Same printed on it, which is the word the printed page uses. The swap control is 180 by 48 under each mat at 174,566 and at 750,566, and it reverses the order of the cards on that mat alone without touching the other. A bracket jaw 210 by 24 rides under any pair of addend rows on a three card mat, hinged at its left end; closing it adds that pair there and then, turns the two cards face down and stands one new card in their place, so a grouping changes without a single number being rewritten. The step bay is 1086 by 110 at 64,620: the number window 420 by 72 at its left, five amount keys 108 by 56 along its middle reading nothing, one, ten, a hundred and a thousand, and the hold the rest control at its right, which drives a small ink pin into every digit that is to stay still. On the third and fourth phases the two mats fold to a single line of their last answer and the step bay grows upward to 1086 by 300 at 64,430, which is the only change of furniture anywhere in the tool; the place chart is then drawn in behind the number as five ruled columns with their headings printed small along the foot, and the column whose digit is about to move lights amber before it moves. In free play the ring bay opens in place of the mats: a triangle 420 by 380 centred at 574,300 with a circle 92 across at each of its three corners and one on the middle of each of its three sides, six in all, and a side total printed along each side, rewritten the moment a card lands in a circle. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a sum or a number has to be written, with a thirteenth key that writes a run of zeros so a round total can be finished in one press. On the fourth phase a strip of five place words, ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten thousands, sits under the keys, because the digit that is going to move is named before the amount key is pressed. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number being added is deep blue, the sum under the rule is green, a carried digit is vermilion and always drawn small above the column it is being added into, a rounded number and any estimated sum are rose, the digit under discussion or the one that is missing is amber, and a zero holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading over it before it is told by its band, and a carry is told by being small and sitting above the rule.
writeup.finish: The card shows one sum worked two ways with its answers together, and the number from the step bay with the digit that moved still lit.

phases.win: both answers land together and read the same
phases.does: works both mats and reads the two answers against each other
phases.goal: swapping the addends leaves the sum alone
phases.says: Swap them over and add again. Did anything change?
phases.check: Away from the screen: add two numbers, then swap them round and add them again. What changed, and what did not?
phases.feels: swapping the two addends over feels as though it must matter, and both sum rows fill with the same number at the same moment
phases.hands: Write the two numbers on two paper slips, add them on squared paper, then swap the slips over and add them again on the line underneath, and read the two answers straight down the page.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: are the same two cards on both mats? Second rung, the phase's: which column is each digit standing in? Third rung: the mats are cut to one digit card apiece and that pair is added both ways round. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: every worked sum in the chapter so far has had the longer number on top, so that looks like part of the method rather than a habit.
wrong.move: writes the larger addend on top on both mats, tidying the swap away while setting the second sum out.
wrong.screen: the right mat clears and refills from the tray in the order the cards were dealt, one card to a row, each ringed in ink as it lands so the order can be read off the mat; both sums are then worked down the columns from the ones and the two answers stand together in the compare rail. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the top row used to be the longer number, and the left hand edge is where a written line begins.
wrong.move: lines the two addends up by their left ends once the shorter one has been swapped to the top.
wrong.screen: the heading over every digit of the shorter card is named under it as the card slides, and the card carries on sliding right until its last digit stands in the ones column, leaving its left hand column standing empty rather than closing the gap up. The rule and the sum row stay empty the whole time it moves, so nothing is added until the places agree.

phases.screen: the same two cards on both mats, in opposite orders
phases.soWhat: The sum is the same whichever order the addends are written in, so the easier one may go on top.
phases.concept: The order of the addends does not matter

phases.win: the two mats agree, and the bracketed pair on one of them makes a round number
phases.does: closes the brackets around the pair that makes a round number
phases.goal: any pair may be added first, and one pair is easier than the others
phases.says: Pick the easiest pair to add first. You are allowed to.
phases.check: You have 4,300 and 15,842 and 5,700 to add. Which two would you add first, and what does that pair make?
phases.feels: you are allowed to choose, and one of the choices makes most of the sum disappear
phases.hands: Write three numbers on three cards, lay them on the table, and let the child draw a pencil loop round whichever pair they want to add first, add that pair out loud, and only then bring the third card in.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which two of your three cards make a round number together? Second rung, the phase's: what is left to add once that bracket is closed? Third rung: the mat is cut to the two cards that make the round number and the third is held in the tray until that pair is done. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: a written sum is read from the left, so the order the cards are lying in looks like an instruction about what has to be done first.
wrong.move: adds the three cards strictly from left to right because that is the order they were dealt.
wrong.screen: the bracket jaw opens under each possible pair in turn with that pair's total printed beside it, so the three first steps stand together on the stage: 2,600 and 7,400 make 10,000 and neither of the other pairs makes anything round, and the jaw under the round pair stays open while the others close. Nothing on the mat is cleared.

wrong.why: the pair total is a new number on the mat, and every number on the mat has been an addend until now.
wrong.move: closes the bracket and then adds the pair total in as well as the two cards it replaced.
wrong.screen: the two bracketed cards turn face down and slide under the single card that replaced them, so three cards are plainly two; the running count at the top left drops to the cards now standing, and the sum row stays empty until the mat holds exactly the cards it is going to add.

phases.screen: three cards on each mat with brackets open around different pairs
phases.soWhat: Three or more addends may be grouped any way at all, so the pair that makes a round number is the pair to add first.
phases.concept: The grouping of the addends does not matter either

phases.win: the number sits unchanged after zero and stands at its successor after one
phases.does: adds each in turn and watches what moves
phases.goal: zero leaves a number alone and one gives its successor
phases.says: Adding nothing leaves it alone. Adding one steps it forward. Which is which?
phases.check: What is 3,67,204 plus nothing, and what is the number straight after 76,409?
phases.feels: adding nothing turns out to be a real addition, and adding one turns out to be a step rather than a sum
phases.hands: Say a number out loud and have the child say the one that comes straight after it, then write both down one under the other and look at which columns are different and which are not.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which column did the amount go into? Second rung, the phase's: how many digits may one column hold? Third rung: the step bay is cut to a three digit number with only the keys for nothing and for one live, and each is pressed on its own. The pad stays open and nothing already written is taken away.

wrong.why: adding is the thing that makes a number bigger, and putting a zero on the end is the one way of making a number bigger that needs no counting at all.
wrong.move: writes the zero onto the end of the number, so 84,376 is handed in as 84,3760.
wrong.screen: the zero is carried down into the ones column where it belongs and sits there in grey, because it is holding a place and bringing no amount, and every column is then read out from the ones with nothing added to any of them. The number in the window is printed twice, before and after, and the two printings are the same.

wrong.why: one more than nine is ten, and ten is the number the child has just said out loud.
wrong.move: adds one to a number ending in nine and writes ten in the ones place.
wrong.screen: the ones column opens to show the ten it has been handed, ten counters standing in a line, and they tie themselves into one bundle that will not fit in a column that holds a single digit; the bundle rides up as a small vermilion one above the tens column, the ones place is left with a grey zero, and the tens column is added again with that carried one in it.

phases.screen: the step bay with a number in it and the amounts zero and one waiting
phases.soWhat: Zero leaves a number exactly as it was, and one gives the number that comes straight after it, which is its successor.
phases.concept: Adding zero changes nothing and adding one steps forward

phases.win: the named digit lifts, the rest stay pinned and the place chart agrees
phases.does: names the digit that will move before pressing, then presses
phases.goal: each round amount raises the digit in its own place and no other
phases.says: Which digit is going to move this time? Say it before you press.
phases.check: A tank held 17,435 L and a thousand litres more went in. Which digit changes, and what does the tank hold now?
phases.feels: the digit that moves is named by the chart and not by where it happens to sit on the line
phases.hands: Write a five digit number with a finger width between the digits, write the place name under each one, and ask which of those names the amount being added belongs to before anybody adds anything at all.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which place does the amount you are adding belong to? Second rung, the phase's: which column on the chart carries that name? Third rung: the chart is cut to that one column with every other digit pinned and greyed, so only that digit is free to move. The place words stay open under the pad.

wrong.why: a thousand is the biggest amount on the keys, and the digit that gets raised is picked by eye rather than read off the chart, which puts it one place out.
wrong.move: adds a thousand by raising the hundreds digit, so 26,318 is handed in as 26,418.
wrong.screen: the place chart slides in behind the number and the thousands column lights amber with its heading named aloud; the hundreds digit the child moved is put back and pinned with the rest, and the thousands digit alone lifts, rolls forward by one and drops, leaving 27,318 in the window. Both numbers stay printed, one under the other.

wrong.why: the shortcut has worked on every number it has been tried on, and in all of those the digit happened to be second along from the left hand end.
wrong.move: adds a thousand to a six digit number by raising the second digit from the left, which is where the thousands digit stood in every five digit number so far.
wrong.screen: a five digit number and a six digit one are stood one under the other with the place chart behind both, and a thousand is added to each; the thousands column lights amber in both, and the two amber digits are plainly not the same distance from the left hand end while both are the fourth column counted in from the right. Nothing is marked and nothing is cleared.

phases.screen: the step bay with the place chart behind the number and every other digit pinned
phases.soWhat: Adding ten raises the tens digit, a hundred the hundreds digit and a thousand the thousands digit, whatever the rest of the number looks like.
phases.concept: Adding ten, a hundred or a thousand lifts one digit

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment one is added to a number that ends in nines. The ones digit rolls forward, reaches ten, cannot stay in a column that holds one digit, and hands the step on: the four nines of 59,999 roll over one after another from the right, each leaving a grey zero behind it because a zero there is holding a place open and bringing nothing, and the roll runs out at the ten thousands column, where the five steps quietly up to six. The window is left reading 60,000, which is the number that comes straight after the one that was standing there. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the two mats stand side by side with the same two cards on each, dealt in opposite orders, their columns ruled under their headings, their rules drawn and their sum rows empty. On the second each mat holds three cards and a bracket jaw lies open under a different pair on each, so the two groupings are showing before anything is pressed. On the third the mats have folded to one line apiece and the step bay has grown up into their place, a number standing in its window with the amount keys for nothing and for one waiting beside it. On the fourth the place chart is drawn in behind that number and every digit carries its small holding pin. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the swap control on the first phase, the open bracket jaw on the second, or the number in the step bay window on the last two, gives one slow pulse while the voice says there are two mats and one set of cards. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any numbers on either mat, brackets anywhere, with the step bay and the ring bay open alongside. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on order, grouping, adding zero and one, and lifting the digit that belongs to the amount.
voiceLines: Two mats, one set of cards. Put the same numbers on both.
Swap them over and add again. Did anything change?
Pick the easiest pair to add first. You are allowed to.
Adding nothing leaves it alone. Adding one steps it forward. Which is which?
Which digit is going to move this time? Say it before you press.
The same kind of sum. Something else is allowed to change.
Free play. Any numbers, either mat, brackets anywhere, and the ring of circles open.
Work both mats again and read the two answers side by side.
You moved the addends about and the sum never budged, and then you lifted one digit on purpose.

observations.why: Only the order of the addends changed, and an order is not an amount.
observations.soWhat: I may write whichever addend is easier to work with on top.
observations.observe: The two mats held the same two cards in opposite orders and their sum rows filled with the same number.

observations.why: Any pair may be added first, so the pair that makes a round number can be picked on purpose.
observations.soWhat: Grouping is not a sentence to recite. It is a way of making the sum in front of me easier.
observations.observe: Closing a bracket turned three cards into two, and one of the two was a round number.

observations.why: Zero puts no amount into any place, so there is nothing for a column to take.
observations.soWhat: Adding zero is still an addition, and its answer is the number you started with.
observations.observe: Adding nothing left every column exactly as it was, and the window printed the number twice the same.

observations.why: A round amount goes into its own place, and a place is named by the chart rather than counted from the left hand end.
observations.soWhat: The shortcut is about a place, so it keeps working however long the number gets.
observations.observe: A thousand raised the fourth column counted in from the right in a five digit number and in a six digit one.

serves.exercise: filling in the blanks when one, ten, a hundred and a thousand are added
arranging the six given numbers in the circles so that every side of the triangle makes nine hundred
stating whether the petrol tank claim is true or false after a thousand litres are added

source_tool.description: The stage carries two mats side by side and one set of number cards that belongs to both. Cards dragged onto the left mat can be dragged onto the right in a different order or a different grouping, and both mats work their sums at once so the two answers land together and can be read against each other. Brackets can be closed around any pair on a three card mat, which adds that pair first and holds the result as a single card, so a grouping can be changed without the numbers being rewritten. A step bay takes one number and a small amount to add to it, and lifts exactly one digit while every other digit is held still: adding ten lifts the tens digit, a hundred the hundreds, a thousand the thousands, and the place chart behind the number names the place as it lifts. Adding nothing lifts nothing, and adding one steps the whole number forward to its successor. A ring bay holds six number cards in a triangle of circles and totals each side as the cards are moved, so an arrangement where every side makes the same total can be hunted rather than guessed.
source_tool.art_direction: Two mats and one tray of cards / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.note: THERE IS NO MODE AXIS ON THIS TOOL FAMILY. learn, practice and freeplay are gone and are not replaced by three of anything else: the axis itself is wrong for a tool a child works alone. See phase_mount.

authored.freeplay: Free Play. Any numbers on either mat, brackets anywhere, the step bay and the ring bay open.
authored.practice: Practice, child alone. Eight items on order, grouping, adding zero and one, and lifting the right digit.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that tie themselves together, a rule under the last addend, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A sum is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the addends stacked with their right ends aligned, and a horizontal rule between the last addend and the sum. A bare row of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach adding.
A carried digit is always drawn small, above the column it is being added into, never in the margin and never below the rule.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number being added is deep blue, the sum under the rule is green, and a digit carried into the next column is vermilion, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A rounded number and any estimated sum are rose, so an estimate is told apart from an exact answer before either is read. The digit under discussion, which is usually the one that is missing, is amber. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a carry is told apart by being small and sitting above its column before it is told apart by its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Work both mats again and read the two answers side by side.
voice.onNext: The same kind of sum. Something else is allowed to change.
voice.opening: Two mats, one set of cards. Put the same numbers on both.
voice.onFinish: You moved the addends about and the sum never budged, and then you lifted one digit on purpose.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any numbers, either mat, brackets anywhere, and the ring of circles open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: The order of the addends does not matter
The grouping of the addends does not matter either
Adding zero changes nothing and adding one steps forward
Adding ten, a hundred or a thousand lifts one digit

placement.where: After the two tanks have been added both ways on paper, so the two answers are already known to match. The tool is what lets a grouping be changed without the numbers being written out again.

answer_key.rule: The sum is the same whichever order the addends are written in, and the same however three or more of them are grouped, so any pair may be added first and the pair that makes a round number is worth choosing. Adding zero leaves a number exactly as it was. Adding one gives the number just after it, its successor. Adding ten raises the tens digit, adding a hundred raises the hundreds digit and adding a thousand raises the thousands digit, and which digit that is depends on the place, not on how long the number is.
answer_key.wrong: The two mats work their sums again side by side, and in the step bay the place chart slides in behind the number with the place that should have moved named. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Working 51,270 + 26,418 down the columns gives 77,688 as well.
The two answers are the same, which is what the order property says.
items.answer: Both give 77,688, so the order of the addends does not change the sum
items.question: Add 26,418 and 51,270, then swap the addends and add again. What do you notice?
items.checkpoint: The sum stays the same whichever order the addends are written in.
items.misconception: Believing the larger addend has to be written on top for the sum to come out right.

steps: Look for a pair that makes a round number: 2,600 + 7,400 = 10,000.
Close the bracket around that pair and hold 10,000 as one card.
Then 10,000 + 18,530 = 28,530, which is easier than working left to right.
items.answer: 28,530, by adding 2,600 and 7,400 first to make 10,000
items.question: Add 2,600 + 7,400 + 18,530 by choosing the easiest grouping.
items.checkpoint: Grouping can be chosen, and the pair that makes a round number is the one to pick.
items.misconception: Thinking three addends have to be added strictly in the order they are written.

steps: Adding zero puts nothing into any column, so the number is unchanged at 84,376.
Adding one raises the ones digit from 6 to 7.
That gives 84,377, which is the successor of 84,376.
items.question: What is 84,376 + 0, and what is 84,376 + 1?
items.checkpoint: Zero leaves a number alone and one gives the number just after it.
items.misconception: Writing 84,3760 for the sum with zero, by putting the zero on the end of the number.

steps: Adding a thousand raises the digit in the thousands place, which here is 6.
That makes the thousands digit 7 and leaves every other digit alone, giving 27,318.
26,418 is what adding a hundred would give, because it raises the hundreds digit instead.
items.answer: No. The tank holds 27,318 L, because adding a thousand raises the thousands digit
items.question: A tank held 26,318 L of water and another 1000 L was poured in. A child wrote 26,418 L. Is that right?
items.checkpoint: A round amount raises the digit in its own place, whatever the number looks like.
items.misconception: Adding a thousand by raising the hundreds digit, which is exactly what gives 26,418.

items.question: Does 34,205 + 18,640 give the same answer as 18,640 + 34,205?
Add 4,300 + 15,842 + 5,700 by choosing the easiest pair first.
items.final_answer: 25,842, by adding 4,300 and 5,700 first to make 10,000

items.question: Add 10 to 48,362, then add 100 to your answer, and say which digit changed each time.
items.final_answer: 48,372 after the ten and 48,472 after the hundred. The tens digit changed first, then the hundreds digit

items.question: A shop had 34,652 packets and a thousand more arrived. A child wrote 34,752. Correct the child and say what went wrong.
items.final_answer: It should be 35,652. The child raised the hundreds digit, but adding a thousand raises the thousands digit

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: works the same cards as two sums at once and stands the answers together
reverses the order of the addends on one mat
closes a bracket around a pair and adds that pair first
adds zero, one, ten, a hundred or a thousand and lifts one digit
names the place of the digit that moved, behind the number
pins every other digit still while one lifts
holds six cards in a triangle of circles and totals every side

teaching_notes: Show each rule before naming it, exactly as the page does. Add the two tanks both ways on paper first, let the class see the answers match, and only then say what happened. For grouping, hand out three numbers where one pair makes a round total and let them choose, because a grouping property that is never used to make a sum easier is a sentence rather than a tool. In the step bay, make them name the digit that will move before they press. Naming it first is the whole difference between a place rule and a shape rule. Then spend real time on the true or false question the page closes on: the wrong answer printed in it is the one most children reach for, and the right correction is not that the arithmetic slipped but that the wrong place was raised. The ring bay carries the triangle puzzle from the earlier page, and it is a grouping question in disguise: the three corner numbers each count towards two sides, so the hunt is really about which three numbers go in the corners.
generation_prompt: Build an addition properties tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Two ruled column mats side by side share one tray of number cards, and both mats work their sums at once so their answers land together for comparison. A swap control reverses the order of the addends on a mat. On a three card mat, brackets can be closed around any pair, which adds that pair first and holds the result as a single card, so a regrouping happens without the numbers being rewritten. A step bay below takes one number and an amount of zero, one, ten, a hundred or a thousand, and animates exactly one digit lifting while a hold the rest control pins every other digit visibly still, with a place value chart sliding in behind the number to name the place that moved. Adding one steps the whole number to its successor with the rollover drawn where it happens. A ring bay holds six number cards in a triangle of three corner circles and three side circles, totalling each side live as cards are moved between circles. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put the same numbers on both mats in different orders and add them together. Close a bracket around whichever pair is easiest and add that pair first. In the step bay, say which digit will move before you add ten, a hundred or a thousand, then press and see whether you were right.
